items.stem: What is a rhetorical question?
options: A question asked by an expert
A question that must be answered in writing
A question asked for effect, without expecting an answer
A question at the end of an exam
items.answer: A question asked for effect, without expecting an answer
items.markingKey: E.g. ‘Is that really the legacy we want to leave?’

items.stem: Explain the effect of the words ‘a glittering mountain of waste’ in this line from a persuasive article from a school magazine, ‘Ditch the Plastic Bottle’: ‘a glittering mountain of waste that will outlive every one of us’
items.answer: the image exaggerates the scale of the waste; ‘glittering’ ironically makes rubbish look attractive while ‘outlive’ stresses how long it lasts.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: 1 for an accurate meaning or connotation of ‘a glittering mountain of waste’. Model point: the image exaggerates the scale of the waste; ‘glittering’ ironically makes rubbish look attractive while ‘outlive’ stresses how long it lasts. Credit any valid interpretation supported by the words.

items.stem: In a persuasive article from a school magazine, ‘Ditch the Plastic Bottle’ the writer uses the metaphor ‘a glittering mountain of waste’: ‘a glittering mountain of waste that will outlive every one of us’ Explain what it suggests to the reader.
items.answer: the image exaggerates the scale of the waste; ‘glittering’ ironically makes rubbish look attractive while ‘outlive’ stresses how long it lasts.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: 1 for an accurate meaning or connotation of ‘a glittering mountain of waste’. Model point: the image exaggerates the scale of the waste; ‘glittering’ ironically makes rubbish look attractive while ‘outlive’ stresses how long it lasts. Credit any valid interpretation supported by the words.

items.stem: Read ‘No stories, no atlases, no dictionaries.’ from a charity appeal, ‘Give a Child a Book’. Name the language feature, quote the key words and explain how they shape the reader’s response.
items.answer: Rule of three (‘No stories, no atlases, no dictionaries’): the repeated ‘no’ in a list of three emphasises how much is missing and builds a sense of loss.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for naming the technique (rule of three); 1 for selecting the key words ‘No stories, no atlases, no dictionaries’; remaining mark(s) for analysis of the effect, e.g. the repeated ‘no’ in a list of three emphasises how much is missing and builds a sense of loss.

items.stem: Read ‘Don’t wait for someone else to act.’ from a charity appeal, ‘Give a Child a Book’. Name the language feature, quote the key words and explain how they shape the reader’s response.
items.answer: Imperative (‘Don’t wait’): the command creates urgency and makes the reader feel guilty if they do nothing.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: 1 for naming the technique (imperative); 1 for selecting the key words ‘Don’t wait’; remaining mark(s) for analysis of the effect, e.g. the command creates urgency and makes the reader feel guilty if they do nothing.

items.stem: Analyse how the writer uses language in these two quotations from a charity appeal, ‘Give a Child a Book’: (i) ‘Close your eyes and picture a classroom with no books.’ (ii) ‘Don’t wait for someone else to act.’ Identify a technique in each and explain its effect.
items.answer: (i) Imperative: commanding the reader to imagine makes them experience the lack of books personally. (ii) Imperative: the command creates urgency and makes the reader feel guilty if they do nothing.
items.markingKey: Award up to 4 marks from: for each quotation, 1 for the technique (imperative; imperative) and 1 for an explanation of its effect; remaining mark(s) for a developed point linking both to the mood or purpose of the text.

items.stem: Read a persuasive article from a school magazine, ‘Ditch the Plastic Bottle’. ‘Every day, our school throws away more than four hundred plastic bottles. Four hundred! Imagine them piled in the playground: a glittering mountain of waste that will outlive every one of us. Is that really the legacy we want to leave? Some people say that recycling solves the problem, but only a small fraction of all the plastic ever made has been recycled. The rest is buried, burned or washed into the sea, where it chokes turtles and breaks down into tiny fragments that end up in the fish we eat. The solution is simple, cheap and fair: install free water fountains and give every student a refillable bottle. Other schools in our city have already done it. We can do it too, and we must start now.’ How does the writer try to persuade students to support refillable bottles? Support your answer with close reference to the text.
items.answer: Statistic and repetition (four hundred!); imperative ‘Imagine’; metaphor of a glittering mountain; rhetorical question; counter-argument rebutted; emotive turtles; rule of three; inclusive ‘we’ and urgent ending.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10 (reading). Top band (7–10): perceptive, well-developed analysis of how the writer uses language and structure to create effects; precise, well-chosen references; sustained focus on the question; middle band (4–6): clear explanation of some effects with relevant references; some analysis of particular words and phrases; lower band (1–3): some relevant points, mostly retelling the text; few references; little comment on language. Indicative content: Statistic and repetition (four hundred!); imperative ‘Imagine’; metaphor of a glittering mountain; rhetorical question; counter-argument rebutted; emotive turtles; rule of three; inclusive ‘we’ and urgent ending.

items.stem: Read a charity appeal, ‘Give a Child a Book’. ‘Close your eyes and picture a classroom with no books. No stories, no atlases, no dictionaries. In parts of the world, this is not imaginary; it is every school day. Amal is ten. She walks five kilometres to school each morning and shares one tattered reader with six classmates. She dreams of being a doctor. For just five dollars a month, you can put a library in her classroom. Five dollars: less than the price of a cinema ticket. Your gift will buy books, train teachers and light up young minds. Don’t wait for someone else to act. Give today, and give a child a future.’ How does the writer use language to persuade readers to donate? Support your answer with close reference to the text.
items.answer: Imperatives; rule of three; anecdote of Amal; emotive ‘tattered’; direct address and minimising cost (‘just five dollars’, cinema ticket); metaphor ‘light up young minds’; urgent ending.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 12 (reading). Top band (9–12): perceptive, well-developed analysis of how the writer uses language and structure to create effects; precise, well-chosen references; sustained focus on the question; middle band (5–8): clear explanation of some effects with relevant references; some analysis of particular words and phrases; lower band (1–4): some relevant points, mostly retelling the text; few references; little comment on language. Indicative content: Imperatives; rule of three; anecdote of Amal; emotive ‘tattered’; direct address and minimising cost (‘just five dollars’, cinema ticket); metaphor ‘light up young minds’; urgent ending.

items.stem: Which sentence uses the rule of three?
options: Our parks should be clean, safe and welcoming.
Our parks are dirty and unsafe.
items.answer: Our parks should be clean, safe and welcoming.
items.markingKey: Three linked adjectives give rhythm and emphasis.

items.stem: What is a fact?
options: A statement of what someone believes
A statement that can be checked and proved true or false
A statement that uses emotive language
A statement that everyone agrees with
items.answer: A statement that can be checked and proved true or false
items.markingKey: Facts can be verified; opinions express beliefs or judgements.

items.stem: Read this sentence from a news article: ‘Protesters swarmed the town hall, screeching their demands.’ Explain how the writer’s choice of words shows bias.
items.answer: The loaded words ‘swarmed … screeching’ create a negative or exaggerated impression rather than simply reporting what happened, so the reader is pushed towards the writer’s view.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: 1 for identifying loaded words (swarmed … screeching); 1 for their connotations; a further mark for the intended effect on the reader.

items.stem: Read this sentence from a news article: ‘The council wants to fill the gardens with concrete ramps and teenagers shouting at all hours.’ Explain how the writer’s choice of words shows bias.
items.answer: The loaded words ‘teenagers shouting at all hours’ create a negative or exaggerated impression rather than simply reporting what happened, so the reader is pushed towards the writer’s view.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for identifying loaded words (teenagers shouting at all hours); 1 for their connotations; a further mark for the intended effect on the reader.

items.stem: Rewrite this sentence in neutral, unbiased language. ‘The greedy developers are bulldozing our precious woodland.’
items.answer: Model: ‘The developers are clearing part of the woodland to build houses.’
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: Award for removing loaded words and keeping the facts. Accept any version that meets the instruction and keeps the meaning; deduct for new errors.

items.stem: A journalist wants to sound impartial. Rewrite this sentence in neutral, unbiased language. Explain one change you made. ‘The greedy developers are bulldozing our precious woodland.’
items.answer: Model: ‘The developers are clearing part of the woodland to build houses.’
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: Award for removing loaded words and keeping the facts. Accept any version that meets the instruction and keeps the meaning; deduct for new errors.

items.stem: Write two short news reports about a city introducing a charge for cars entering the centre: one biased in favour and one biased against. Then write a short paragraph explaining the techniques you used to create bias in each. Write about 250–350 words in total.
items.answer: Model approach: same core facts in both; report 1 uses positive loaded words, favourable quotations and selected facts; report 2 uses negative loaded words, critical quotations and omits benefits; commentary names the techniques (loaded language, selection, ordering, quotation choice, headline).
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10: Content and structure 6 marks, Style and accuracy 4 marks. Content and structure – top band (5–6): both reports share the facts but are clearly and skilfully biased in opposite directions; commentary precisely explains selection, loaded language, ordering and headlines; middle band (3–4): two recognisably different reports with some loaded language; commentary identifies some techniques; lower band (1–2): reports barely differ or ignore facts; little explanation. Style and accuracy – top band (3–4): precise, often ambitious vocabulary chosen for effect; a wide range of sentence structures used deliberately; register consistently suited to audience and purpose; spelling, punctuation and grammar almost always accurate; middle band (2): generally appropriate vocabulary with some ambition; some variety of sentence structure; register mostly suitable; occasional errors that do not obscure meaning; lower band (1): simple or repetitive vocabulary; limited sentence variety; register may slip; frequent errors in spelling, punctuation or grammar that sometimes obscure meaning. Indicative content: selection and omission of facts; connotations of word choice; which quotations are included; headline framing; order of information.

items.stem: Read this from a balanced article, ‘Should Phones Be Banned in Schools?’: ‘Supporters of a ban argue that phones distract students in lessons and that social media can make bullying worse.’ Give one argument used by supporters of a ban.
items.answer: Phones distract students in lessons
items.markingKey: Retrieval: the answer is stated in the quotation (‘Supporters of a ban argue that phones distract students in lessons and that social media can make bullying worse.’).

items.stem: In a balanced article, ‘Should Phones Be Banned in Schools?’ the writer writes: ‘On the other hand, many parents want their children to carry a phone’ What is the function of ‘On the other hand’ in the article?
items.answer: It signals a turn from the arguments for a ban to the arguments against, showing the reader that the other side is now being considered.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: contrast/signals the counter-view; links the two halves of the argument

items.stem: In a balanced article, ‘Should Phones Be Banned in Schools?’ the writer writes: ‘A compromise may be the best solution’ Why does the writer suggest a compromise near the end?
items.answer: After weighing both sides, the writer offers a solution that takes account of each, which shows balance and leads to a reasoned conclusion.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: reaches a judgement after weighing both sides; shows fairness/balance

items.stem: A student writes: ‘Homework should be banned because students need time to relax.’ Write two or three sentences that present a counter-argument to this claim and then rebut it.
items.answer: Model: Some argue that homework is essential for practice. While practice matters, short, focused tasks in school could achieve the same benefit without exhausting students.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for a fair counter-argument; 1 for a rebuttal with a reason; remaining mark(s) for appropriate discourse markers (however, admittedly, nevertheless) and clear expression.

items.stem: A student writes: ‘Everyone should become vegetarian to protect the planet.’ Write two or three sentences that present a counter-argument to this claim and then rebut it.
items.answer: Model: Critics say that meat is an important source of protein and part of many cultures. Admittedly this is true, yet reducing meat rather than banning it would still cut emissions while respecting traditions.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: 1 for a fair counter-argument; 1 for a rebuttal with a reason; remaining mark(s) for appropriate discourse markers (however, admittedly, nevertheless) and clear expression.

items.stem: A student writes: ‘Zoos should be closed because animals belong in the wild.’ Write two or three sentences that present a counter-argument to this claim and then rebut it.
items.answer: Model: Supporters of zoos point out that they protect endangered species through breeding programmes. Nevertheless, these programmes could be run in sanctuaries that give animals far more space.
items.markingKey: Award up to 4 marks from: 1 for a fair counter-argument; 1 for a rebuttal with a reason; remaining mark(s) for appropriate discourse markers (however, admittedly, nevertheless) and clear expression.

items.stem: Write a balanced argument answering the question ‘Should the school day start later?’ Present both sides fairly, use evidence and reach a reasoned conclusion. Write about 250–350 words.
items.answer: Model plan for ‘Should the school day start later?’: introduction; strongest arguments for; strongest arguments against; weighing/compromise; conclusion giving a clear, justified view.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10: Content and structure 6 marks, Style and accuracy 4 marks. Content and structure – top band (5–6): both sides explored fairly and in depth with evidence; points weighed against each other; a reasoned judgement reached in the conclusion; cohesive paragraphing; middle band (3–4): both sides covered with some development; structure clear though weighing of points is limited; lower band (1–2): mainly one side or a list of points; little development or evaluation. Style and accuracy – top band (3–4): precise, often ambitious vocabulary chosen for effect; a wide range of sentence structures used deliberately; register consistently suited to audience and purpose; spelling, punctuation and grammar almost always accurate; middle band (2): generally appropriate vocabulary with some ambition; some variety of sentence structure; register mostly suitable; occasional errors that do not obscure meaning; lower band (1): simple or repetitive vocabulary; limited sentence variety; register may slip; frequent errors in spelling, punctuation or grammar that sometimes obscure meaning. Indicative content: introduction setting out the issue; paragraphs for and against with evidence; counter-arguments and rebuttals; discourse markers; reasoned conclusion.

items.stem: In a balanced argument, a paragraph begins ‘Admittedly,’ Explain how this phrase guides the reader through the argument.
items.answer: Concedes a point to the other side before the writer answers it, which makes the writer seem fair.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: identifies the function of the phrase (concedes a point to the other side before the writer answers it, which makes the writer seem fair); explains how it helps the reader follow the structure of the argument.

items.stem: In a formal debate, what is the side that supports the motion called?
items.answer: proposition
items.markingKey: Proposition supports the motion; opposition argues against it.

items.stem: Explain the effect of this line from a student’s speech to the school council, ‘Give Us a Quiet Room’: ‘Where did you go?’
items.answer: the question makes listeners recall their own frustration, so they relate to the problem.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: 1 for an accurate meaning or connotation of ‘Where did you go?’. Model point: the question makes listeners recall their own frustration, so they relate to the problem. Credit any valid interpretation supported by the words.

items.stem: ‘we are not asking for luxury. We are asking for a space to think.’ (a student’s speech to the school council, ‘Give Us a Quiet Room’). What does the phrase ‘We are asking’ suggest, and how might it make the reader feel?
items.answer: the repeated structure creates a memorable contrast and a strong, rhythmic ending.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for an accurate meaning or connotation of ‘We are asking’; 1 for the effect on the reader, mood or idea created. Model point: the repeated structure creates a memorable contrast and a strong, rhythmic ending. Credit any valid interpretation supported by the words.

items.stem: Identify the technique used in ‘we are not asking for luxury. We are asking for a space to think.’ (a student’s speech to the school council, ‘Give Us a Quiet Room’) and analyse its effect on the reader.
items.answer: Repetition (‘We are asking’): the repeated structure creates a memorable contrast and a strong, rhythmic ending.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for naming the technique (repetition); 1 for selecting the key words ‘We are asking’; remaining mark(s) for analysis of the effect, e.g. the repeated structure creates a memorable contrast and a strong, rhythmic ending.

items.stem: Identify the technique used in ‘the canteen sounds like a football stadium’ (a student’s speech to the school council, ‘Give Us a Quiet Room’) and analyse its effect on the reader.
items.answer: Hyperbole (‘like a football stadium’): the exaggerated comparison makes the noise vivid and adds humour, keeping listeners engaged.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: 1 for naming the technique (hyperbole); 1 for selecting the key words ‘like a football stadium’; remaining mark(s) for analysis of the effect, e.g. the exaggerated comparison makes the noise vivid and adds humour, keeping listeners engaged.

items.stem: Write a speech for the proposition in a school debate on the motion ‘This house would replace exams with coursework.’ Write about 250–350 words.
items.answer: Model structure: greeting and stance (proposition); point 1 with evidence; point 2 with an anecdote; rebuttal of the strongest opposing point; call to the audience to vote.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10: Content and structure 6 marks, Style and accuracy 4 marks. Content and structure – top band (5–6): a clear purpose and point of view; strong, consistent sense of audience; rhetorical devices used purposefully; well-signposted structure with an effective opening and ending; middle band (3–4): clear purpose with some awareness of audience; some rhetorical devices; structure mostly clear; lower band (1–2): purpose unclear; little sense of a listening audience; few devices; loosely organised. Style and accuracy – top band (3–4): precise, often ambitious vocabulary chosen for effect; a wide range of sentence structures used deliberately; register consistently suited to audience and purpose; spelling, punctuation and grammar almost always accurate; middle band (2): generally appropriate vocabulary with some ambition; some variety of sentence structure; register mostly suitable; occasional errors that do not obscure meaning; lower band (1): simple or repetitive vocabulary; limited sentence variety; register may slip; frequent errors in spelling, punctuation or grammar that sometimes obscure meaning. Indicative content: formal greeting; clear stance; signposted points with evidence; rhetorical devices; rebuttal of the other side; memorable conclusion.

items.stem: What is emotive language?
options: Words chosen to provoke a strong emotional reaction
items.answer: Words chosen to provoke a strong emotional reaction
items.markingKey: E.g. ‘chokes turtles’, ‘tattered’.

items.stem: In a persuasive article from a school magazine, ‘Ditch the Plastic Bottle’ the writer uses the statistic ‘more than four hundred’: ‘Every day, our school throws away more than four hundred plastic bottles.’ Explain what it suggests to the reader.
items.answer: a precise, large number makes the problem seem real and shocking, and gives the argument authority.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: 1 for an accurate meaning or connotation of ‘more than four hundred’. Model point: a precise, large number makes the problem seem real and shocking, and gives the argument authority. Credit any valid interpretation supported by the words.

items.stem: Write two sentences that persuade classmates to read more books. One of them must use an anecdote. Underline or name the technique and explain why it would persuade the reader.
items.answer: Any two persuasive sentences in which one is a clear anecdote (a short personal story used to support a point), with a valid explanation of its persuasive effect.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for an accurate anecdote; 1 for persuasive purpose clearly served; remaining mark(s) for explaining the effect on the reader.

items.stem: Write a charity appeal persuading readers to donate to an animal rescue centre. Write about 250–350 words.
items.answer: Model structure: hook (question or striking fact); problem; two or three reasons with evidence and emotive detail; counter-argument rebutted; call to action.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10: Content and structure 6 marks, Style and accuracy 4 marks. Content and structure – top band (5–6): a clear, sustained point of view; well-developed reasons supported by evidence; counter-arguments anticipated and rebutted; logical, cohesive paragraphs and a strong conclusion; middle band (3–4): a clear view with some supporting reasons and evidence; some development; paragraphs mostly logical; lower band (1–2): a simple view with few or undeveloped reasons; limited organisation. Style and accuracy – top band (3–4): precise, often ambitious vocabulary chosen for effect; a wide range of sentence structures used deliberately; register consistently suited to audience and purpose; spelling, punctuation and grammar almost always accurate; middle band (2): generally appropriate vocabulary with some ambition; some variety of sentence structure; register mostly suitable; occasional errors that do not obscure meaning; lower band (1): simple or repetitive vocabulary; limited sentence variety; register may slip; frequent errors in spelling, punctuation or grammar that sometimes obscure meaning. Indicative content: clear persuasive purpose; a range of techniques (rhetorical question, rule of three, emotive language, statistics, direct address, counter-argument); structured paragraphs; strong call to action.

items.stem: Read a newspaper opinion column, ‘Skate Park Plan Is a Disaster Waiting to Happen’. ‘The council’s plan to build a skate park beside Jubilee Gardens is, quite simply, madness. The gardens are one of the last peaceful places in our town, loved by families, pensioners and wildlife alike. Now the council wants to fill them with concrete ramps and teenagers shouting at all hours. The park will cost $250,000. Local residents were consulted in a survey last spring, but only 300 people replied. Everyone I have spoken to is against it. Supporters claim the park will keep young people off the streets, but in my experience bored teenagers will cause trouble wherever they are. The council should listen to the people who actually pay for it, before it is too late.’ How does the writer try to turn readers against the skate park, and how far is the article biased?
items.answer: Loaded words (madness, disaster); stereotypes of teenagers; one-sided selection; a fact undermined by ‘only’; unrepresentative ‘everyone I have spoken to’; dismissive counter-argument; final appeal to taxpayers.
items.markingKey: Level-marked: top band (4–5) perceptive analysis with precise references; middle (2–3) clear explanation of some effects; lower (1) mainly retelling. [5]

items.stem: Which of these statements is a fact rather than an opinion?
options: Teenagers today are lazier than ever.
Homework is the worst part of school life.
The film is far too long and boring.
items.answer: The match ended 2–1.
items.markingKey: ‘The match ended 2–1.’ can be checked and proved; the others are judgements.

items.stem: Read this sentence from a news article: ‘A gang of youths loitered outside the shop.’ Explain how the writer’s choice of words shows bias.
items.answer: The loaded words ‘gang … loitered’ create a negative or exaggerated impression rather than simply reporting what happened, so the reader is pushed towards the writer’s view.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: 1 for identifying loaded words (gang … loitered); 1 for their connotations; a further mark for the intended effect on the reader.

items.stem: Read a travel feature, ‘Paradise Found at Azure Bay’: ‘Forget every holiday you have ever had. Azure Bay is, without doubt, the most beautiful resort on the planet. Its 150 luxury rooms overlook a private beach of powder-white sand, and the hotel’s three restaurants serve food that will make you weep with joy. Families adore the kids” club; couples adore the sunset spa. Yes, the nearest town is a two-hour drive away, but why would you ever want to leave? Rooms start at $400 a night, a small price for perfection. Every guest I met said it was the best week of their lives. Book now, before the rest of the world discovers it.’ Identify two facts and two opinions in the text, and explain how the writer uses facts to support their bias.
items.answer: Facts: 150 rooms; three restaurants; the nearest town is two hours away; rooms start at $400 a night. Opinions: the most beautiful resort on the planet; food that will make you weep with joy; a small price for perfection. The writer brushes aside the remote location and the high price, quotes only delighted guests and gives no independent reviews.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 per correct fact/opinion; credit explanation of framing (‘only’), stereotyping, unrepresentative evidence, missing viewpoints.

items.stem: In a balanced argument, a paragraph begins ‘Critics of this idea point out that’ Explain how this phrase guides the reader through the argument.
items.answer: Introduces a counter-argument and attributes it to others, keeping the tone balanced.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: identifies the function of the phrase (introduces a counter-argument and attributes it to others, keeping the tone balanced); explains how it helps the reader follow the structure of the argument.

items.stem: In a balanced article, ‘Should Phones Be Banned in Schools?’ the writer writes: ‘Ultimately, the aim should be to teach students to use technology responsibly rather than simply to remove it.’ What is the writer’s final view?
items.answer: The writer believes education about responsible use is better than a total ban; ‘Ultimately’ signals this considered conclusion.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: final view stated; reference to ‘Ultimately’ or ‘rather than simply to remove it’

items.stem: Write a five-paragraph plan for a balanced argument answering the question ‘Should children be paid for doing household chores?’ Give a one-line summary of each paragraph.
items.answer: Model plan: 1 Introduction – the issue and why it matters; 2 Arguments for, with evidence; 3 Arguments against, with evidence; 4 Weighing the strongest points / possible compromise; 5 Conclusion – reasoned judgement.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: introduction; points for; points against; evaluation; conclusion with judgement; logical order.

items.stem: In a student’s speech to the school council, ‘Give Us a Quiet Room’ the writer uses the counter-argument ‘Some of you may say’: ‘Some of you may say there is no spare room. But the old music store has been empty since September.’ Explain what it suggests to the reader.
items.answer: anticipating the objection and answering it with a practical fact makes the speaker seem prepared and reasonable.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: 1 for an accurate meaning or connotation of ‘Some of you may say’. Model point: anticipating the objection and answering it with a practical fact makes the speaker seem prepared and reasonable. Credit any valid interpretation supported by the words.

items.stem: Rewrite this written sentence so that it would work well in a speech to students. ‘Some people disagree with this view.’
items.answer: Model: ‘Now, some of you may be thinking, ‘That will never work.’ Let me show you why it can.’
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: Award for features of spoken persuasion: direct address, rhetorical question, signposting, rhythm; appropriate register. Accept any version that meets the instruction and keeps the meaning; deduct for new errors.

items.stem: Rewrite this written sentence so that it would work well in a speech to students. ‘Sport is beneficial for health and concentration.’
items.answer: Model: ‘Who here feels sharper after a game at break? Exactly. Sport wakes up our bodies and our brains.’
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: Award for features of spoken persuasion: direct address, rhetorical question, signposting, rhythm; appropriate register. Accept any version that meets the instruction and keeps the meaning; deduct for new errors.

items.stem: Which of these is an example of direct address?
options: You can make a difference today.
items.answer: You can make a difference today.
items.markingKey: Direct address speaks to the reader as ‘you’.

items.stem: Explain the effect of the words ‘chokes turtles’ in this line from a persuasive article from a school magazine, ‘Ditch the Plastic Bottle’: ‘where it chokes turtles and breaks down into tiny fragments that end up in the fish we eat’
items.answer: the distressing image of suffering animals and contaminated food stirs pity and fear, making readers want to act.

items.stem: Identify the technique used in ‘Everyone I have spoken to is against it.’ (a newspaper opinion column, ‘Skate Park Plan Is a Disaster Waiting to Happen’) and analyse its effect on the reader.
items.answer: Anecdote (‘Everyone I have spoken to’): a personal, unrepresentative sample is presented as if it were proof, which is misleading.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for naming the technique (anecdote); 1 for selecting the key words ‘Everyone I have spoken to’; remaining mark(s) for analysis of the effect, e.g. a personal, unrepresentative sample is presented as if it were proof, which is misleading.

items.stem: Write a letter to your local council persuading them to improve the bus service for young people. Write about 250–350 words.
items.answer: Model structure: hook (question or striking fact); problem; two or three reasons with evidence and emotive detail; counter-argument rebutted; call to action.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10: Content and structure 6 marks, Style and accuracy 4 marks. Content and structure – top band (5–6): form and register fully appropriate (greeting, purpose stated early, sign-off); points developed and well ordered; tone consistently suited to the reader; middle band (3–4): recognisable letter form; points clear with some development; tone mostly suitable; lower band (1–2): form inconsistent; points brief or unclear; tone unsuited to the reader. Style and accuracy – top band (3–4): precise, often ambitious vocabulary chosen for effect; a wide range of sentence structures used deliberately; register consistently suited to audience and purpose; spelling, punctuation and grammar almost always accurate; middle band (2): generally appropriate vocabulary with some ambition; some variety of sentence structure; register mostly suitable; occasional errors that do not obscure meaning; lower band (1): simple or repetitive vocabulary; limited sentence variety; register may slip; frequent errors in spelling, punctuation or grammar that sometimes obscure meaning. Indicative content: clear persuasive purpose; a range of techniques (rhetorical question, rule of three, emotive language, statistics, direct address, counter-argument); structured paragraphs; strong call to action.

items.stem: Write an advertisement for a new after-school club, persuading students to join. Write about 350–450 words.
items.answer: Model structure: hook (question or striking fact); problem; two or three reasons with evidence and emotive detail; counter-argument rebutted; call to action.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 12: Content and structure 7 marks, Style and accuracy 5 marks. Content and structure – top band (5–7): a clear, sustained point of view; well-developed reasons supported by evidence; counter-arguments anticipated and rebutted; logical, cohesive paragraphs and a strong conclusion; middle band (3–4): a clear view with some supporting reasons and evidence; some development; paragraphs mostly logical; lower band (1–2): a simple view with few or undeveloped reasons; limited organisation. Style and accuracy – top band (4–5): precise, often ambitious vocabulary chosen for effect; a wide range of sentence structures used deliberately; register consistently suited to audience and purpose; spelling, punctuation and grammar almost always accurate; middle band (2–3): generally appropriate vocabulary with some ambition; some variety of sentence structure; register mostly suitable; occasional errors that do not obscure meaning; lower band (1): simple or repetitive vocabulary; limited sentence variety; register may slip; frequent errors in spelling, punctuation or grammar that sometimes obscure meaning. Indicative content: clear persuasive purpose; a range of techniques (rhetorical question, rule of three, emotive language, statistics, direct address, counter-argument); structured paragraphs; strong call to action.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) What is a fact? (b) What does it mean if a text is biased?
items.answer: (a) A statement that can be checked and proved true or false (b) It presents a one-sided view, favouring one side unfairly
items.markingKey: (a) Facts can be verified; opinions express beliefs or judgements. (b) Bias: selective facts, loaded words, ignoring the other side.

items.stem: ‘The council’s plan to build a skate park beside Jubilee Gardens is, quite simply, madness.’ (a newspaper opinion column, ‘Skate Park Plan Is a Disaster Waiting to Happen’). What does the phrase ‘madness’ suggest, and how might it make the reader feel?
items.answer: the extreme, loaded word dismisses the plan without evidence and pushes the reader to share the writer’s anger.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: 1 for an accurate meaning or connotation of ‘madness’; 1 for the effect on the reader, mood or idea created; 1 for a developed point that explores a second connotation or links to the wider text. Model point: the extreme, loaded word dismisses the plan without evidence and pushes the reader to share the writer’s anger. Credit any valid interpretation supported by the words.

items.stem: A journalist wants to sound impartial. Rewrite this sentence in neutral, unbiased language. Explain one change you made. ‘The minister finally admitted that the scheme had collapsed.’
items.answer: Model: ‘The minister said the scheme had not met its targets.’
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: Award for removing loaded words and keeping the facts. Accept any version that meets the instruction and keeps the meaning; deduct for new errors.

items.stem: In a balanced argument, a paragraph begins ‘Nevertheless,’ Explain how this phrase guides the reader through the argument.
items.answer: Shows that, despite the point just made, the writer still holds their view.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: identifies the function of the phrase (shows that, despite the point just made, the writer still holds their view); explains how it helps the reader follow the structure of the argument.

items.stem: Explain why a balanced argument should include a counter-argument even when the writer has a clear view.
items.answer: It shows the writer has considered other perspectives, makes the argument fairer and more convincing, and allows the writer to rebut objections.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: fairness/credibility; chance to rebut.

items.stem: A student writes: ‘Video games are a waste of time.’ Write two or three sentences that present a counter-argument to this claim and then rebut it.
items.answer: Model: Some claim games improve problem-solving and teamwork. This may be true for some games, but the hours spent could also be used for exercise or reading, so limits are sensible.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for a fair counter-argument; 1 for a rebuttal with a reason; remaining mark(s) for appropriate discourse markers (however, admittedly, nevertheless) and clear expression.

items.stem: Write a balanced argument answering the question ‘Should every student learn a musical instrument?’ Present both sides fairly, use evidence and reach a reasoned conclusion. Write about 250–350 words.
items.answer: Model plan for ‘Should every student learn a musical instrument?’: introduction; strongest arguments for; strongest arguments against; weighing/compromise; conclusion giving a clear, justified view.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10: Content and structure 6 marks, Style and accuracy 4 marks. Content and structure – top band (5–6): both sides explored fairly and in depth with evidence; points weighed against each other; a reasoned judgement reached in the conclusion; cohesive paragraphing; middle band (3–4): both sides covered with some development; structure clear though weighing of points is limited; lower band (1–2): mainly one side or a list of points; little development or evaluation. Style and accuracy – top band (3–4): precise, often ambitious vocabulary chosen for effect; a wide range of sentence structures used deliberately; register consistently suited to audience and purpose; spelling, punctuation and grammar almost always accurate; middle band (2): generally appropriate vocabulary with some ambition; some variety of sentence structure; register mostly suitable; occasional errors that do not obscure meaning; lower band (1): simple or repetitive vocabulary; limited sentence variety; register may slip; frequent errors in spelling, punctuation or grammar that sometimes obscure meaning. Indicative content: introduction setting out the issue; paragraphs for and against with evidence; counter-arguments and rebuttals; discourse markers; reasoned conclusion.

items.stem: Explain the effect of the words ‘seven out of ten’ in this line from a student’s speech to the school council, ‘Give Us a Quiet Room’: ‘A recent survey of our Year 9 found that seven out of ten students feel stressed during exam season.’
items.answer: the figure provides evidence and makes the problem seem widespread rather than personal.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: 1 for an accurate meaning or connotation of ‘seven out of ten’. Model point: the figure provides evidence and makes the problem seem widespread rather than personal. Credit any valid interpretation supported by the words.

items.stem: Identify the technique used in ‘A recent survey of our Year 9 found that seven out of ten students feel stressed during exam season.’ (a student’s speech to the school council, ‘Give Us a Quiet Room’) and analyse its effect on the reader.
items.answer: Statistic (‘seven out of ten’): the figure provides evidence and makes the problem seem widespread rather than personal.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for naming the technique (statistic); 1 for selecting the key words ‘seven out of ten’; remaining mark(s) for analysis of the effect, e.g. the figure provides evidence and makes the problem seem widespread rather than personal.

items.stem: Read ‘we are not asking for luxury. We are asking for a space to think.’ from a student’s speech to the school council, ‘Give Us a Quiet Room’. Name the language feature, quote the key words and explain how they shape the reader’s response.
items.answer: Repetition (‘We are asking’): the repeated structure creates a memorable contrast and a strong, rhythmic ending.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: 1 for naming the technique (repetition); 1 for selecting the key words ‘We are asking’; remaining mark(s) for analysis of the effect, e.g. the repeated structure creates a memorable contrast and a strong, rhythmic ending.
